title: Frustration-Aggression Theory
summary: How hardship breeds aggression, why that aggression lands on weak and outnumbered groups, and what the theory can and cannot explain.

lesson.title: When hard times turn hostile
lesson.hook: A man's boss cuts his salary. He says nothing at work, then shouts at his children over a spilled cup of garri that evening. Why them, and not the boss?

slides.heading: A motivational account
slides.body:
**Frustration-aggression theory** explains prejudice through **motivation**: when people face hardship, they become more likely to criticise and attack out-groups.

The idea comes from **Dollard, Doob, Miller, Mowrer and Sears (1939)** at Yale, who proposed that **frustration**, being blocked from a goal, produces an urge to aggress. Hard times, the theory predicts, are hostile times.

slides.heading: Generalised aggression
slides.body:
Frustration does not produce a neat, targeted response. It raises **generalised aggression**: a readiness to lash out at almost anyone.

That is why we sometimes snap at the very people we love. The anger is real, but it is not really about them. It spills over from a frustration somewhere else.

slides.question: According to frustration-aggression theory, aggression tends to rise when people:
slides.why: Frustration means being blocked from a goal, and the theory says this raises aggression. Easy success and security reduce it.

slides.heading: The salary cut
slides.story: Mr Okafor's company cuts salaries just as food prices rise. He cannot shout at the managing director without risking his job. At home, he becomes harsh with his children over small things: noise, a dirty plate, a late return from school. His frustration is real, but its source is out of reach.
slides.takeaway: Frustration from one source can raise aggression that is released somewhere safer.

slides.heading: Cotton prices and lynchings
slides.body:
**Carl Hovland and Robert Sears (1940)** looked at records from the American South. They found a **negative correlation** between the **price of cotton** in a year and the **number of lynchings** of Black Americans that year.

When cotton fetched little and farmers struggled, lynchings rose; in good years, they fell. Economic frustration seemed to turn into violence against a vulnerable group.

slides.question: Hovland and Sears (1940) found that as cotton prices fell, lynchings:
slides.why: The negative correlation means low prices went with more lynchings: lean times, more violence.

terms.meaning: The state of being blocked from reaching a goal
A broad readiness to lash out, not aimed at one target
As one measure goes down, the other goes up
Explaining prejudice by needs and drives, not beliefs alone

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'briefly explain frustration-aggression theory' and the cotton study. The favourite trap is the direction of the correlation: students write 'positive' because both 'go with' hardship. Cotton price and lynchings moved in opposite directions, so the correlation is negative.
slides.sampleQuestion: Hovland and Sears (1940) reported a ______ correlation between cotton prices and lynchings: (a) positive (b) negative (c) zero (d) curvilinear
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (b): as prices fell, lynchings rose. Then explain this supports the idea that hardship increases aggression toward weak groups.

points: Frustration-aggression theory is a motivational account of prejudice.
Dollard and colleagues (1939): frustration produces an urge to aggress.
Frustration raises generalised aggression, even towards loved ones.
Hovland and Sears (1940): cotton prices fell, lynchings rose.

questions.stem: Frustration-aggression theory offers which kind of account of prejudice?
questions.explanation: It explains prejudice through drives and needs triggered by hardship, so it is a motivational account.

questions.stem: In frustration-aggression theory, 'frustration' means:
questions.explanation: Frustration is the blocking of goal-directed behaviour, which the theory links to aggression.

questions.stem: The cotton price study was carried out by:
questions.explanation: Carl Hovland and Robert Sears published the cotton price and lynching analysis in 1940.

questions.stem: The theory predicts that during times of hardship, aggression will:
questions.explanation: Hardship is frustrating, and frustration raises aggression.

questions.stem: 'Generalised aggression' means aggression that:
options: Is aimed only at the cause of frustration
Is a broad readiness to lash out at many targets
questions.explanation: Frustration produces a general readiness to aggress, not one focused only on its source.

questions.stem: The relationship Hovland and Sears found between cotton prices and lynchings was:
questions.explanation: Lower prices went with more lynchings, a negative correlation. Correlation alone does not prove cause.

questions.stem: After failing her driving test, Bisi snaps at her younger brother for asking a simple question. This best illustrates:
questions.explanation: Her frustration from the test spills over onto someone uninvolved, which is generalised aggression.

questions.stem: A researcher finds that hate crimes against migrants rise in years when unemployment rises. This pattern is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: Economic hardship producing more aggression towards a vulnerable group fits frustration-aggression theory, like the cotton study.

questions.stem: In a good harvest year in the cotton study, the theory would predict:
questions.explanation: Good times mean less frustration and so less aggression. 'No lynchings at all' overstates it.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Hovland and Sears findings is MOST accurate?
options: They showed a correlation consistent with the theory
They proved that low prices cause lynchings
questions.explanation: It was archival correlational data, so it supports but cannot prove causation. The correlation was negative.

questions.stem: Frustration-aggression theory was first set out by:
questions.explanation: Dollard, Doob, Miller, Mowrer and Sears proposed it in 1939. Sears later co-authored the cotton study.

questions.stem: All of the following are consistent with frustration-aggression theory EXCEPT:
options: Aggression rises in hard economic times
Aggression is always aimed at the true source of frustration
questions.explanation: The theory stresses that aggression is often not aimed at the true source. That is the point of generalised and displaced aggression.

questions.stem: I. Frustration raises generalised aggression. II. The cotton study showed a negative correlation. III. The theory explains prejudice mainly through beliefs about groups. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and II are correct. III is wrong: it is a motivational account, not one based mainly on beliefs.

questions.stem: Why is frustration-aggression theory described as 'motivational' rather than 'cognitive'?
options: It focuses on how people store stereotypes
It is based on social categories
It explains prejudice by a drive aroused by blocked goals
questions.explanation: It locates the cause in a drive or urge produced by frustration. Cognitive accounts focus on beliefs and categories.

questions.stem: A critic notes that some frustrated people respond by working harder or withdrawing, not by aggressing. This criticism suggests that:
options: Frustration does not always lead to aggression
Aggression always has a frustration cause
questions.explanation: Frustration can lead to many responses, so the original claim that it always leads to aggression is too strong. It does not mean frustration never causes aggression.

lesson.title: Hitting the safe target
lesson.hook: When fuel queues stretch for hours, people rarely march on the refinery. They curse the pump attendant, the okada rider, or 'those people'. Who gets blamed, and why them?

slides.heading: Displacement
slides.body:
Often we **cannot attack the true source** of our frustration. It may be too powerful, too vague (like 'the economy'), or attacking it would bring bigger trouble.

So the aggression is **displaced**: redirected onto a **safer target**. This is **displaced aggression**, and it is the element that makes the theory relevant to discrimination.

slides.heading: Why minorities become targets
slides.body:
Who counts as 'safe'? Groups that are **outnumbered** and in a **weaker position**. They are less able to fight back, so hostility against them carries little cost.

The theory therefore predicts that hardship will produce **malice directed at minority groups**. It does not just say aggression rises; it says **where** the aggression goes: towards the relatively powerless.

slides.question: Displaced aggression is aggression that is:
options: Aimed at the true source of frustration
Redirected onto a safer, often weaker target
slides.why: Displacement means shifting the aggression from a risky source to a safer target. Aiming at the true source is direct aggression.

slides.heading: The scapegoat
slides.body:
The word comes from an ancient ritual in which the community's sins were symbolically placed on a goat that was then driven away. A **scapegoat** today is a person or group **blamed for problems they did not cause**.

**Scapegoating** combines displaced aggression with blame: 'prices are high because of them'. Minority traders, migrants and religious minorities have often played this role in history.

slides.heading: Blaming the stranger
slides.story: In a town hit by job losses, rumours spread that a small migrant community is 'taking all the jobs'. In truth, a factory closed because of import costs. But the factory owners are far away and powerful, while the migrants are few and nearby. Market stalls owned by migrants are attacked one night.
slides.takeaway: The frustration comes from the factory closure, but aggression is displaced onto a weaker, outnumbered group.

slides.heading: Insecurity and stereotyping
slides.body:
From displacement, it is a small step to a wider prediction: people **stereotype more and give in to prejudice** when they feel **insecure** or when their **self-esteem is threatened**.

A threatened ego looks for someone to feel superior to. Putting down an out-group can restore a sense of control and worth, which links this theory to social identity ideas.

slides.heading: Limits of the theory
slides.body:
The original claim that frustration **always** leads to aggression proved too strong. Neal **Miller (1941)** softened it: frustration produces several responses, of which aggression is one.

Leonard **Berkowitz** (1989) later argued frustration leads to aggression mainly when it creates **negative feelings**, and that cues in the environment can trigger it. The theory also struggles to explain **why one particular group** is chosen as the target.

slides.question: Which of the following is a recognised weakness of frustration-aggression theory?
options: It cannot fully explain why a particular group becomes the target
It is based only on minimal groups
slides.why: The theory says weak groups are targeted, but not why one weak group rather than another. That gap needed other theories, such as stereotypes and norms.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: 'Explain the concept of displaced aggression' appears often. Define it, explain why the true source is avoided, and say why minorities are targeted: outnumbered, weaker, safe. Then link it to discrimination. The trap: confusing displaced aggression with generalised aggression. Generalised is the spread; displaced is the redirection.
slides.sampleQuestion: Frustration-aggression theory predicts that hardship will produce hostility mainly towards: (a) the powerful source of frustration (b) outnumbered and weaker groups (c) the government only (d) one's own family only
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (b): weaker, outnumbered groups are safe targets. In an essay, use the cotton study and a Nigerian scapegoating example.

points: Displaced aggression shifts anger from a risky source to a safer target.
Weak, outnumbered minorities are the usual safe targets.
Displacement is what links the theory to discrimination.
Scapegoats are blamed for problems they did not cause.
Revisions: frustration does not always produce aggression (Miller; Berkowitz).

questions.stem: Displaced aggression is aggression directed at:
questions.explanation: Displacement redirects aggression from a risky source to a safer target.

questions.stem: According to the theory, minority groups are often targeted because they are:
options: Outnumbered and in a weaker position
questions.explanation: Being outnumbered and weaker makes them safe targets for displaced aggression.

questions.stem: A group blamed for problems it did not cause is called a:
questions.explanation: A scapegoat carries blame for troubles caused by others.

questions.stem: What element makes frustration-aggression theory relevant to discrimination?
questions.explanation: Displacement explains why aggression lands on weak out-groups, linking frustration to discrimination.

questions.stem: People often cannot aggress against the true source of frustration because:
options: The source is always a minority
questions.explanation: The real source is often powerful or vague, so attacking it would cause more trouble.

questions.stem: The theory predicts people stereotype more when they:
options: Feel insecure or their self-esteem is threatened
questions.explanation: Threat and insecurity push people towards stereotypes and prejudice.

questions.stem: Workers angry at a bank's loan rejection attack the shops of a small immigrant community instead. This is:
questions.explanation: The anger comes from the bank but lands on a weaker group, which is displacement.

questions.stem: During a fuel scarcity, residents blame 'Hausa traders' for high prices, though the cause is national supply problems. The traders are acting as:
questions.explanation: They are blamed for a problem they did not cause, which is scapegoating.

questions.stem: A student humiliated by a lecturer later mocks a weaker student from another ethnic group. Frustration-aggression theory would say he chose that target because it was:
options: Safe, with little risk of retaliation
questions.explanation: Displaced aggression goes to a target that cannot easily strike back.

questions.stem: The difference between generalised and displaced aggression is that displaced aggression:
options: Is redirected from the true source to a substitute target
questions.explanation: Generalised aggression is a broad readiness to lash out; displaced aggression specifically shifts it to a substitute.

questions.stem: Neal Miller (1941) revised the original theory by arguing that:
options: Frustration can produce several responses, aggression being one
questions.explanation: Miller weakened the 'always' claim: aggression is one of several possible responses to frustration.

questions.stem: All of the following are criticisms or limits of frustration-aggression theory EXCEPT:
options: It ignores the role of hardship
It does not explain why a specific group is chosen
Frustration does not always produce aggression
Environmental cues and feelings also matter
questions.explanation: Hardship is central to the theory, so ignoring it is not a limit. The others are real criticisms.

questions.stem: I. Displacement makes the theory relevant to discrimination. II. The theory specifies the direction of hostility in hard times. III. The theory fully explains why one minority rather than another is targeted. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and II are correct. III is false: choosing one minority over another needs other explanations, such as stereotypes and social norms.

questions.stem: Berkowitz's revision suggests frustration leads to aggression especially when it:
options: Produces negative feelings and aggressive cues are present
questions.explanation: Berkowitz linked aggression to negative affect plus cues in the environment, refining the original theory.

questions.stem: A researcher finds that in a recession, hostility rises towards a small, poor minority but not towards a small, wealthy and well-connected minority. This best supports the idea that displaced aggression targets groups that are:
options: Highly visible in the media only
questions.explanation: Both groups are small, but only the weak one is targeted. Power and the ability to retaliate, not size alone, decide the 'safe' target.
